about: Maps three.js APIs to their null3D equivalents. Each entry gives a status, the first engine version and a docs page ID.

statusLegend.direct: Same concept; the call or option changes name only.
statusLegend.changed: Supported, with a different API or pattern. Follow the note.
statusLegend.manual: Must be rewritten by hand, for example GLSL shaders or render hooks.
statusLegend.post-1.0: Not in version 1.0. Use the workaround in the note.
statusLegend.unsupported: Out of scope for null3D. Use the workaround in the note.

sinceLegend.0.1: the core renderer, with cameras, materials, lights and shadows
sinceLegend.0.2: content, such as glTF models, animation, raycasting and post-processing
sinceLegend.0.3: developer tools, such as the `null3d` command, templates and the porting tools

entries.target: createEngine({ canvas, sketch }) on the page; scene code moves to sketch.ts inside defineSketch()
entries.notes: The engine picks WebGPU or WebGL2 itself. antialias: true maps to createEngine({ antialias: 'msaa' }) and false to 'none'; without the option the quality preset picks FXAA on Low and MSAA 4x from Medium up; alpha: true maps to createEngine({ transparent: true }); powerPreference maps to createEngine({ powerPreference }), whose default is 'high-performance'.

entries.target: createEngine({ maxPixelRatio }) and the quality presets; quality.set({ maxPixelRatio }) in the sketch
entries.notes: The engine sizes the canvas to its CSS size times the screen's pixel ratio, up to the quality preset's cap. The option replaces the cap, and quality.set changes it during play.

entries.three: renderer.setSize / window resize handler / camera.aspect + updateProjectionMatrix
entries.target: Automatic
entries.notes: The engine follows the canvas's CSS size. Perspective cameras, and orthographic cameras made with a height, follow its aspect ratio in every frame. Delete resize handlers and updateProjectionMatrix calls.

entries.target: onUpdate(dt) returned from defineSketch()
entries.notes: The engine renders every frame by itself; never call a render function. Per-frame logic goes in onUpdate, camera-follow logic in onLateUpdate.

entries.target: castShadows: true on the light; the shadowFilter quality setting sets the filter
entries.notes: PCFShadowMap and PCFSoftShadowMap become the shadowFilter setting: 3 x 3 or 5 x 5 texels, by preset. quality.set({ shadowFilter }) changes it during play. BasicShadowMap and VSMShadowMap have no equivalent.

entries.three: renderer.toneMapping (ACESFilmic, AgX, Neutral, Reinhard, Cineon, Custom, Linear) / toneMappingExposure
entries.target: post.set({ toneMapping: 'agx' | 'agx-punchy' | 'neutral' | 'aces' | 'none' | curveWgsl, exposure })
entries.notes: The engine default is "agx-punchy", AgX with Filament's punchy look; three.js defaults to no tone mapping, so ports of scenes without it set toneMapping: "none". A port keeps the curve it set: AgXToneMapping becomes "agx" and ACESFilmicToneMapping "aces". The curves use three.js's formulas. "none" applies the exposure, as LinearToneMapping does; NoToneMapping ignores toneMappingExposure, so keep exposure at 1 when porting it. Copy toneMappingExposure to exposure unchanged: null3D multiplies it into each light rather than into the finished picture, which gives the same image, and bloom's threshold keeps its meaning. A scene in real units sets ev100 instead, and exposure then acts as exposure compensation. ReinhardToneMapping and CineonToneMapping become the reinhard and cineon curves of @null3d/three-compat: post.set({ toneMapping: reinhard }), with three.js's formulas. CustomToneMapping becomes a custom tone curve: post.set({ toneMapping: wgsl }), where the WGSL declares fn toneCurve(color: vec3f) -> vec3f. Leave out the curve's multiply by toneMappingExposure, because the color arrives exposed. A custom curve needs HDR color, as bloom does, so compatibility mode draws in HDR color with FXAA while one is set; a device without an HDR target keeps the built-in curve.

entries.target: Nothing to do
entries.notes: Output is sRGB with a linear working space, as in three.js r152+ defaults: the final pass encodes sRGB and dithers. Hex colors are sRGB and [r, g, b] arrays are linear, as three.js reads them. Delete these lines.

entries.target: debug.stats(true), or createEngine({ stats: true }) on the page; debug.frameStats() for numbers
entries.notes: The overlay shows the frame rates, CPU time per thread and phase, draw calls and uploads, the GPU tier, the preset and the render scale. From 0.2 it sits at the canvas's top right, and its header shows the frame rate. A click opens a card with each thread's and the GPU's time against the target frame rate, triangles and objects drawn, and the memory of the engine, the GPU's textures and buffers, the heap and the page. Triangles count every pass, shadow maps included, as renderer.info.render.triangles does. Objects count the instances of each draw, so an object counts once per pass that draws it. The page shows it with createEngine({ stats: true }), engine.stats(true) or ?stats (0.2). @null3d/engine/stats (0.2) shows a three.js page's own figures in the same panel, with StatsPanel, or as text, with statsText. engine.measure() on the page gives percentiles of CPU and GPU time, and memory. In the sketch, debug.frameStats() (0.2) also gives the textures' GPU bytes, their budget and their dropped mip levels.

entries.target: quality.textureMemory; textures.memoryBytes; the quality setting textureMemoryMiB; debug.frameStats().gpuTextureBytes and gpuBufferBytes
entries.notes: three.js counts the textures that the renderer holds, not their bytes, and sets no budget. null3D reports the textures' GPU bytes and holds them under the preset's budget: past it, textures from files drop their largest mip levels, which load again once room returns. debug.frameStats() (0.2) also gives the bytes of every GPU texture and buffer that the engine holds, render targets and shadow maps included.

entries.target: await scene.warmUp() before hiding the loading screen
entries.notes: The first frame waits for its pipelines. warmUp resolves once every pipeline that the scene needs is built, hidden objects included, so warm up a later loading stage before you show it.

entries.target: scene.setBackground('#rrggbb' | texture | environment (0.2) | cube map (0.2) | { sky } (0.2), options)
entries.notes: A texture fills the view behind every object and stretches to its shape, as a texture background does in three.js. An environment or a cube map surrounds the scene, as a PMREM texture or a CubeTexture in scene.background does. Exposure and tone mapping change the background, as in three.js's WebGPURenderer; WebGLRenderer draws a background color, and an sRGB background texture, without them. For an exact page color, set toneMapping: "none", or use createEngine({ transparent: true }) over a CSS background. setClearColor(color, 0) on an alpha canvas becomes transparent: true with no background.

entries.target: createEngine({ canvas })
entries.notes: Create the canvas in HTML or in page.ts and pass it in. The engine hands it to the render worker.

entries.target: await engine.capture() on the page
entries.notes: Resolves with a PNG Blob of the next frame that the engine draws. Tests read pixels with engine.captureFrame() instead.

entries.target: const pass = render.addPass({ kind: 'scene', camera, writes: 'myTexture', size: [width, height] }); materials.unlit({ map: textures.fromPass(pass) })
entries.notes: Passes are declared, not called: the render graph orders them, runs them only while a texture shows them, and plans their memory. The texture holds linear color after the exposure, upright with v = 0 at the bottom as three.js's render target texture. A pass never draws objects that show its own texture. Scene passes draw point and spot lights and the scene's background, unless a clearColor replaces it, and no ambient occlusion, as three.js's render targets draw none. A light that only a pass sees casts no shadow there. A render target the size of the canvas or a share of it takes scale: 1, 0.5 or 0.25 in place of size, and follows the render size. A render target that a ShaderPass fills becomes a full-screen pass: render.addPass({ kind: 'fullscreen', wgsl, writes, size or scale, textures }).

entries.three: renderer.setViewport / setScissor (split screens, picture in picture)
entries.target: scene.createView({ camera, rect }): one scene drawn again from another camera, into a rectangle of the canvas, after the camera's view
entries.notes: rect is [x, y, width, height] as fractions of the canvas from its top-left corner, so [0.5, 0, 0.5, 1] is its right half. Give each view its own camera; setRect changes the rectangle and allocates nothing, and destroy removes the view. The camera's view draws the whole canvas first, so a split screen that covers the canvas draws the scene once for the camera and once for each view. Each view costs one cull and one scene draw at its rectangle's pixels; the sun's shadows and the lights cost nothing more. A view's objects take no ambient occlusion or screen-space reflections; the camera's volumetric fog and outline reach the whole image, a view's rectangle included. For a minimap that a material shows in the world, a scene pass into a texture (textures.fromPass) is cheaper than a view.

entries.target: engine.capabilities on the page, and ctx.engine.capabilities in the sketch
entries.notes: Reports the GPU tier, limits and features. Never branch on GPU names: some browsers hide them.

entries.target: Nothing to do; createEngine({ largeWorld: true }) and batch origins for planet-scale scenes (0.2)
entries.notes: The engine draws reversed depth in a 32-bit float buffer. On WebGL2 without EXT_clip_control, reversed depth keeps GL's range, which is less precise. engine.capabilities.depth says which depth the device draws. The engine also renders relative to the camera through per-cell offsets. With largeWorld: true, positions that you set keep their full precision at any distance, and createInstances takes an origin that its rows are relative to.

entries.target: The scene from the sketch context: defineSketch(({ scene }) => ...)
entries.notes: Objects are created in the scene directly.

entries.target: scene.setEnvironment(await assets.loadEnvironment('/env/sunset.ktx2'))
entries.notes: `loadEnvironment` takes an HDR file as it is, or its map from `bunx @null3d/cli assets env`, which needs no filtering at load. `pmremGenerator.fromScene(new RoomEnvironment(), 0.04)` becomes `await assets.builtinEnvironment('room')`: the same room with the same blur, made on the GPU as three.js makes it, with no file to download. `pmremGenerator.fromScene(sceneWithSky)` becomes `await assets.skyEnvironment()`, once: its map follows `scene.setBackground({ sky })`, so drop the calls that make the map again after each change. Its map leaves out the sun's disc, whose light the directional light gives. scene.environmentIntensity becomes the `intensity` option.

entries.target: scene.setFog({ curve: 'linear', color, near, far })
entries.notes: The linear curve keeps three.js's smooth step and its defaults of 1 and 1000. null3D measures the straight-line distance from the camera, where three.js measures the depth along the view. So fog at the screen's corners is a little thicker, and it no longer shifts as the camera turns. null3D mixes the fog in linear color before the tone mapping, as WebGPURenderer does, and as WebGLRenderer does when it draws into a half-float target. Only WebGLRenderer's default 8-bit canvas mixes the fog after the sRGB encoding, so there the same fog looks a little darker at middle distances. Materials opt out with fog: false. For new scenes, the default exponential curve looks more like real haze. The fog can also thin with height (heightFalloff) and glow toward the sun (sunGlow).

entries.target: scene.setFog({ curve: 'exp2', color, density })
entries.notes: Pass three.js's density. Its default there is 0.00025, and null3D's is 0.01. null3D measures the straight-line distance from the camera, where three.js measures the depth along the view. So fog at the screen's corners is a little thicker, and it no longer shifts as the camera turns. null3D mixes the fog in linear color before the tone mapping, as WebGPURenderer does, and as WebGLRenderer does when it draws into a half-float target. Only WebGLRenderer's default 8-bit canvas mixes the fog after the sRGB encoding, so there the same fog looks a little darker at middle distances. Materials opt out with fog: false.

entries.target: scene.setFog({ color, density, heightFalloff, volumetric: { intensity, anisotropy, distance } })
entries.notes: three.js has no lit fog in its core. Its webgpu_volume_lighting example marches rays through a box with VolumeNodeMaterial, lit by point and spot lights with shadows. null3D lights the scene's own fog instead, in a grid that follows the camera's view, with the sun's shadow cascades and the point and spot lights' shadows. Drop the box: the fog's density and heightFalloff say where the air holds haze, and its scattering intensity becomes intensity. The god rays effects of add-on libraries blur a mask of the sky toward the sun on the screen. null3D's rays also come from lamps and from shadows off the screen. It draws where the quality setting fogSlices is above 0: Medium and up. On Low the fog keeps its sunGlow.

entries.target: scene.createGroup({ name, position })
child.setParent(parent); setParent(parent, { keepWorld: true }) for attach(); getParent() for object.parent; destroy() to remove
entries.notes: Objects are in the scene as soon as they are created. setParent keeps the local transform, like add(), and getParent() returns an object's parent, or null for a root object. Creating, destroying and re-parenting rebuild the draw tables in that frame, so during play hide with setVisible and pool with setActiveCount instead (guides/performance).

entries.target: obj.setPosition(x, y, z); obj.translate(x, y, z) for translateX/Y/Z
entries.notes: translate moves along the object's own axes, as translateX, translateY and translateZ do together. For many moving objects, use an instance batch and write its positions array directly instead of calling setters.

entries.target: obj.setRotationEuler(x, y, z, 'XYZ'), obj.rotateX/Y/Z(angle), or obj.setRotation(qx, qy, qz, qw)
entries.notes: Euler order strings match three.js. rotateX, rotateY and rotateZ turn the object about its own axes, as in three.js. For rotateOnAxis, multiply the quaternion from obj.getRotation by one from quat.setAxisAngle, and pass the product to setRotation.

entries.target: obj.setRotation(x, y, z, w), with the quaternion from quat.setAxisAngle, quat.fromEuler, quat.multiply or quat.slerp
entries.notes: The quat helpers write into an array that you create once with quat.create(). Pass its four numbers to setRotation. The rotations array of an instance batch takes the same order.

entries.target: obj.setScale(x, y, z)
obj.lookAt(x, y, z)
entries.notes: Meshes and groups turn their +Z axis to the point. Cameras and lights turn their -Z axis there, as in three.js. The call assumes that the object's parents are not rotated.

entries.target: obj.getWorldPosition(out), obj.getWorldQuaternion(out), obj.getWorldMatrix(out)
entries.notes: Each getter copies into an array that you make once, with vec3.create(), quat.create() or mat4.create(). They read the engine's last transform update, so a change made in onUpdate shows in the same frame's onLateUpdate. getWorldMatrix gives 16 numbers, column by column, like matrixWorld.elements.

entries.target: Nothing to do: objects are static by default and update when a setter changes them; create objects that move every frame with dynamic: true
entries.notes: Remove manual matrix calls. Move single objects with their setters. Only instance batches take writes to their typed arrays, and a static batch uploads only the rows you mark with markDirty.

entries.target: scene.find(name) for getObjectByName; your own arrays of objects instead of traverse and children
entries.notes: scene.find returns the first object created with the name, from an index. No call walks an object's children, so keep the objects you need in arrays at setup time.

entries.target: obj.setVisible(false)
entries.notes: Cheap: it uploads the object's matrix and draw entry and never rebuilds the draw tables, so use it instead of removing and adding objects during play. The objects under a hidden object, dynamic ones too, stop updating until it shows again, where three.js updates their matrices anyway. So hide a pool of spare objects under one parent.

entries.target: mesh.setCastShadows(true) / setReceiveShadows(true), or the castShadows and receiveShadows options of createMesh
entries.notes: Both are false by default, as in three.js. The directional light, spot lights and point lights cast them on both GPU paths; point lights where the preset's pointLightShadows is on. Unlit materials show no shadows. An instance batch takes castShadows and receiveShadows in createInstances, or batch.setCastShadows(true) / setReceiveShadows(true), for every row (since 0.2).

entries.target: obj.setLayers(mask), obj.getLayers(), camera.setLayers(mask), batch.setLayers(mask); the layers option of createMesh, createInstances and createPerspectiveCamera
entries.notes: Masks have the same 32 bits and the same default, layer 0 alone, and a camera draws an object when their masks share a bit. layers.set(n) becomes setLayers(1 << n), and layers.mask becomes getLayers(). For enable and disable, read the mask with getLayers() and pass the new mask. An InstancedMesh's layers become its batch's, for every row. Raycasts and declared passes take layer masks from 0.2. Shadow casters differ: three.js tests them against the camera's layers, and null3D against the light's. Give each light that casts shadows the layers of every object that must cast, or those objects cast nothing.

entries.target: mesh.setRenderOrder(n)
entries.notes: Orders blended objects, lower first, before their depth, as in three.js. The engine orders opaque and masked objects itself for speed. The rows of an instance batch sort by depth one by one, where three.js sorts an InstancedMesh as one object.

entries.target: mesh.setFrustumCulled(false)
entries.notes: Usually needed only for shader-displaced geometry; prefer mesh.setBounds(center, radius) with larger bounds, which keeps culling at work.

entries.target: Your own arrays, or a Map keyed by the object
entries.notes: Engine objects have no userData, and their TypeScript types refuse new properties. A Map from each object to its data keeps the data beside the object. Arrays indexed the way your sketch counts objects stay fastest in per-frame loops.

entries.target: onUpdate / onLateUpdate, or a declared pass (0.2)
entries.notes: The engine draws from lists that the sketch records, so it calls no sketch code per draw. Move per-object work into onUpdate or onLateUpdate. Declared passes come with step 0.2.

entries.target: scene.instantiate(prefab) for loaded models; scene.clone(obj) for built objects
entries.notes: Each instantiate shares the model's meshes, materials and textures. scene.clone copies an object and every object below it, lights and cameras included, under the same parent. A copy of an animated model gets an animator of its own, as SkeletonUtils.clone gives a copy its own skeleton.

entries.target: texture.destroy(); material.destroy() (0.2); mesh.destroy() (0.2); prefab.destroy() (0.2) for a loaded glTF model
entries.notes: texture.destroy() frees a texture's GPU memory, and materials that map it draw with their colors alone. material.destroy() (0.2) frees the material's place, and a custom material's pipelines with its last material, once no object uses it; objects that still use it draw nothing. mesh.destroy() (0.2) frees a mesh's GPU memory and data at the next frame, and throws E1111 while an object or instance batch uses it, so destroy those first, in the same frame or before. prefab.destroy() (0.2) frees every mesh, material and texture of a loaded model, and its skeleton and clips, once its copies are destroyed. three.js's dispose leaves the object usable and uploads it again on the next render; null3D's destroy ends it, and later calls throw E1101.

entries.target: scene.overrideMaterial = material, and null for each object's own material
entries.notes: Draws every mesh and instance batch of the main pass with the material, each keeping its mesh, place and instances, as three.js does. Sprites, points, lines and particle systems keep their own materials, and the shadow maps keep each object's material, so a masked caster still cuts its shadow. A sprite, point or line material throws E1224. The change rebuilds the engine's draw tables in the next frame, and adds no draw call or pipeline after that.

entries.target: scene.setEnvironment(env, { rotation }) and scene.setBackground(env, { rotation })
entries.notes: Rotation is an Euler array in radians, in the order X, Y, Z, as in three.js. Each material shares the scene's rotation, so material.envMapRotation has none of its own. scene.setBackground turns environments and cube maps, not textures or the sky.

entries.target: scene.setBackground(env, { blur, intensity })
entries.notes: Each setBackground call sets the options of that background, where three.js keeps them on the scene. The blur reads the environment's level for that roughness, as three.js reads its PMREM texture, so it costs nothing extra. Only environments blur: three.js turns a blurred CubeTexture into a PMREM texture, and the engine asks for an environment from assets.loadEnvironment. intensity applies to textures, environments, cube maps and the sky.

entries.target: scene.createPerspectiveCamera({ fov, near, far, position, target })
entries.notes: fov is vertical and in degrees, as in three.js. The aspect ratio is automatic. The fov, near and far properties are read-only: change them with camera.setFov(degrees) and camera.setNearFar(near, far).

entries.target: camera.setFocalLength(mm) and camera.focalLength
entries.notes: null3D's sensor is a full-frame camera's, 24 mm tall, along the canvas's height, so a focal length gives the same field of view on every canvas shape. three.js measures its filmGauge, 35 mm by default, along the longer side. The two agree on a square canvas with filmGauge 24. Depth of field takes the camera's focal length unless its settings give one.

entries.three: OrthographicCamera(left, right, top, bottom, near, far)
entries.target: scene.createOrthographicCamera({ height, near, far, position, target }), or left, right, top and bottom in place of height
entries.notes: With height alone, the width follows the canvas's aspect ratio, so code that recomputes left and right on resize goes away. The four edges keep their shape on any canvas, as in three.js. To zoom, call camera.setOrthoHeight with the original height divided by three.js's zoom.

entries.target: camera.worldToScreen(point, out) for [x, y, depth]; camera.screenToRay(x, y, ray) for a ray through a point
entries.notes: Both take and give CSS pixels from the canvas's top-left corner, not device coordinates from -1 to 1. The depth is the distance in front of the camera, below 0 behind it. A ray through the pointer's position uses the camera of the frame on screen at the pointer's event. three.js starts an orthographic ray on the camera's plane, and screenToRay starts it on the near plane.

entries.target: scene.createReflectionProbe({ box: { min, max }, position, refresh: 'always' }); a reflection pass for a flat mirror: render.addPass({ kind: 'reflection', writes, plane })
entries.notes: A CubeCamera with a WebGLCubeRenderTarget, filtered by PMREMGenerator and set as a material's envMap, becomes a reflection probe. The probe captures the scene from its position on the GPU and filters it for each roughness. It lights every surface inside its box, not one material, and its box projects the reflections, so walls reflect at their own distance. Give the probe a box around the space that the object moves in. boxProjection: false reads it as three.js reads a cube map, as light from far away. cubeCamera.update() in every frame becomes refresh: 'always'; one update after a change becomes probe.capture(). The near and far of the CubeCamera fall away: captures draw from 5 cm out to the camera's far plane. Leave the reflecting object out of its own probe's captures with layers.

entries.target: None; split screens use scene.createView with one camera for each view
entries.notes: Stereo rendering belongs to XR, which is out of scope.

entries.target: scene.createDirectionalLight({ direction, color, intensity, castShadows, shadow })
entries.notes: The light is an object. Pass the target minus the position as direction, or call light.lookAt(x, y, z), again whenever the target moves. Surfaces show the first directional light created, which casts the shadows. Delete shadow.camera bounds: the engine's shadow cascades fit the view by themselves, and the shadow distance follows the farthest visible receiver by default, so a port with its own shadow.camera.far passes that number as shadow: { distance }. It also draws contact shadows on High and Ultra (0.2), which three.js lacks: set shadow: { contactDistance: 0 } to match three.js's look.

entries.target: scene.createPointLight({ position, color, intensity, range, decay, castShadows, shadow, intensityUnit })
entries.notes: distance becomes range, which every point light needs: 0, a light with no end, is not allowed, because the engine finds the lights near each surface by their ranges. intensity stays in candela. light.power = lumens becomes intensity: lumens with intensityUnit: 'lumen', which divides by 4π as power does; setIntensity then takes lumens.

entries.three: SpotLight(color, intensity, distance, angle, penumbra, decay)
entries.target: scene.createSpotLight({ position, direction | target, angle, penumbra, range, decay, intensity, map, castShadows, shadow, intensityUnit })
entries.notes: distance becomes range, which every spot light needs. intensity stays in candela; light.power = lumens becomes intensity: lumens with intensityUnit: 'lumen', which divides by π at any cone angle, as power does. target is a point: call light.lookAt(x, y, z) when it moves. castShadow becomes castShadows, and shadow takes bias and normalBias in meters. The quality preset sets the tile size in place of shadow.mapSize, and shadow.camera has no equivalent. light.map becomes map: sRGB pixels as { width, height, data }, or setMap(pixels), resampled to 128 x 128 texels and projected by the cone as three.js projects it; its top row follows the world's up, as three.js aims its map's camera, so a light rolled about its axis shows the same map. Up to 32 lights show a map at once.

entries.target: scene.createHemisphereLight({ skyColor, groundColor, intensity })
entries.notes: The sky lies along the light's +Y axis: turn the light to tilt it, where three.js moves it. It lights surfaces as three.js's does, diffuse only, and its light adds to the environment's. Any number of them cost the same per pixel.

entries.target: scene.createAmbientLight({ color, intensity })
entries.notes: Several ambient lights add up.

entries.target: scene.createRectAreaLight({ color, intensity, width, height, range })
entries.notes: Needs a range, where three.js's light has no end. No RectAreaLightUniformsLib.init() call. The light leaves along -Z, as in three.js. Casts no shadows, as in three.js.

entries.target: Nothing: the engine loads the area lights' tables with the first area light
entries.notes: Remove the init() call.

entries.target: scene.setLightProbeGrid: a grid of irradiance probes lights the scene where a surface stands
entries.notes: One LightProbe that lights the whole scene is an environment: scene.setEnvironment takes the diffuse spherical harmonics with the environment map, which `bunx @null3d/cli assets env` computes offline. For light that changes from place to place, bake a grid with bakeProbes and set it with scene.setLightProbeGrid. The grid holds L1 spherical harmonics per probe, where three.js's LightProbeGrid holds L2. The light probe grid section of the scene page shows both calls.

entries.three: LightProbeGrid (addons: a baked grid of L2 irradiance probes)
entries.target: scene.setLightProbeGrid with a grid that bakeProbes bakes in the sketch
entries.notes: three.js's grid stores L2 spherical harmonics per probe. null3D's stores L1, which takes three texture reads per pixel in place of seven. The light keeps its direction, but small bright patches spread a little wider. three.js adds the grid's light to the environment's diffuse light; null3D's grid takes the environment's place. To add it as three.js does, set environmentWeight: 0. Bake the grid again with bakeProbes.

entries.target: Built in: scene.createPointLight and scene.createSpotLight; the engine clusters every light
entries.notes: Delete the add-on and its setup. null3D sorts point and spot lights into clusters on both GPU paths, and they may cast shadows. three.js's add-on takes point lights without shadows, on WebGPU only.

entries.target: Built in: shadow: { cascades } on the directional light
entries.notes: Delete the addon. Its cascades, maxFar and shadowMapSize become the cascades, distance and mapSize settings. The cascades keep still edges as the camera turns, and far cascades draw every few frames, as the farCascadeInterval quality setting says. The fade option is on by default: neighboring cascades blend over a band, which the shadowCascadeBlend quality setting sizes, and fade: false maps to shadowCascadeBlend: 0. The mode setting has no equivalent: the engine's split leans a little more toward the camera than the addon's practical mode, so its near cascade is shorter.

entries.target: scene.createDirectionalLight({ direction, castShadows: true, shadow: { cascades: 2 } })
entries.notes: Delete the add-on. The directional light's shadow takes cascades fitted to the camera's view, with a blend between neighbours. SunLight's two cascades become cascades: 2. The CSM entry maps the other settings.

entries.target: Contact shadows of the directional light: scene.createDirectionalLight({ contactDistance })
entries.notes: Both search the camera's depth toward the main light for short shadows where objects touch. contactDistance sets their reach in meters, 0.3 by default. They draw where the quality setting contactShadowSteps is above 0, as on High and Ultra.

entries.target: shadow: { mapSize, bias, normalBias, cascades, distance } in the directional light's options, or light.setShadow()
entries.notes: mapSize is one number, the texels on each side. bias and normalBias are in meters, where three.js gives bias in depth units, so start from the defaults. The directional light's map stores 16-bit depth, so in each cascade bias covers at least 1.5 of its depth steps, about 2 cm in a far cascade 200 m out. radius and blurSamples become the shadowFilter quality setting, 3 or 5 texels on each side. shadow.camera has no equivalent: the cascades fit the camera's view.

entries.target: Physical light units, as in three.js r155 and later
entries.notes: Scenes tuned in three.js's legacy light mode need new intensities: retune them with parity images.

entries.three: Box / Sphere / Plane / Cylinder / Cone / Torus / Capsule / Circle / Ring Geometry
entries.target: geometry.box({ width, height, depth }), geometry.sphere({ radius }), and one generator for each class
entries.notes: The constructor's arguments become options with the same names and defaults: new CylinderGeometry(0.3, 0.4, 2) is geometry.cylinder({ radiusTop: 0.3, radiusBottom: 0.4, height: 2 }). The meshes match three.js's vertex for vertex, with the same positions, normals, texture coordinates and triangles. Each object has one material, so an array of materials for the face groups of a box or a cylinder needs one object for each group.

entries.three: geometry.rotateX / rotateY / rotateZ / translate / scale / center / applyMatrix4
entries.target: obj.setRotationEuler(x, y, z), obj.setPosition(x, y, z) or obj.setScale(x, y, z) on the object that draws the mesh
entries.notes: A mesh keeps the vertices its generator built, so the transform goes on each object or instance row: floor.setRotationEuler(-Math.PI / 2, 0, 0) lays a plane flat. To build the transform into the vertices, transform the arrays and pass them to geometry.fromArrays.

entries.three: TorusKnot / Icosahedron / Octahedron / Tetrahedron / Dodecahedron / Polyhedron / Lathe / Extrude / Shape / Tube Geometry
entries.target: geometry.fromArrays(torusKnot({ radius, tube, tubularSegments, radialSegments, p, q })), and icosahedron, octahedron, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, polyhedron, lathe, shape, extrude and tube, from @null3d/geometry
entries.notes: Install @null3d/geometry. Each function takes the constructor's arguments as named options with three.js's defaults, and returns arrays with three.js's vertices, normals and texture coordinates for geometry.fromArrays. Shape, Path, the curves and ShapeUtils come with the same names and methods, but points are [x, y] or [x, y, z] arrays, not Vector2 or Vector3. ExtrudeGeometry's caps and sides form one mesh, which takes one material.

entries.target: geometry.fromArrays({ positions, normals, uvs, uvs1, colors, tangents, joints, weights, indices })
entries.notes: Returns a mesh that createMesh and createInstances accept. The attributes position, normal, uv, uv1, color and tangent each become one array, and setIndex becomes indices, 16-bit or 32-bit. The engine copies the arrays. From 0.2, skinIndex and skinWeight become joints and weights, 8-bit and 16-bit integer arrays stay integers on the GPU, and { array, normalized: true } keeps a BufferAttribute's normalized flag.

entries.target: mesh.updateVertices(name, values, start, count)
entries.notes: Pass the attribute's values of every vertex, in the array type the mesh was made with; start and count pick the vertices that change, as addUpdateRange does, but in vertices. The mesh keeps the bounding sphere it was made with, so give objects bounds with setBounds when vertices move outside it. Meshes with joints or morph targets take no updates. For many moving objects, use instances instead of rewriting vertices.

entries.target: geometry.fromArrays({ ..., computeNormals: true, computeTangents: true })
entries.notes: The results match three.js's bit for bit. computeTangents needs uvs, and works without indices too. Bounds are always automatic, so computeBoundingSphere and computeBoundingBox need no call.

entries.target: WireframeGeometry: a material with wireframe: true on the mesh itself. EdgesGeometry: scene.createLines({ positions, mode: 'segments' }) with two points per edge
entries.notes: A wireframe material draws each triangle's three edges, as WireframeGeometry lists them, with no copy of the mesh. null3D does not find a mesh's feature edges for you, as EdgesGeometry does with its angle threshold. Build that list of edge points from the mesh's arrays, or with EdgesGeometry at build time, and draw it as pairs of points.

entries.target: DOM labels (ui.trackLabel), a texture with pre-rendered text, or a text mesh baked into glTF
entries.notes: Not built yet. An add-on that draws text with MSDF fonts comes in step 0.3. Until then, use the target's options.

entries.target: mesh.setMorphWeight(indexOrName, weight) and mesh.getMorphWeight(indexOrName); geometry.fromArrays({ ..., morphTargets: { positions, normals, colors, names } })
entries.notes: glTF morph targets and their default weights load with the model, and its clips animate the weights. Targets are deltas, as with morphTargetsRelative = true. Color targets (morphAttributes.color, glTF's COLOR_0 targets) change vertex colors, which stay between 0 and 1 as glTF asks; three.js does not clamp them. mesh.mesh.morphTargetNames lists the names in target order, in place of morphTargetDictionary. A clip blends its weights with the object's own, as AnimationMixer does. On WebGL2 each object draws only its largest weights, by the morphTargets quality setting: 8 on Low up to 64 on Ultra.

entries.target: materials.standard({ color, map, metalness, roughness, normalMap, aoMap, emissive, ... })
entries.notes: Both follow glTF's metallic-roughness model with the same formulas, so color, metalness, roughness and emissive values carry over. roughnessMap and metalnessMap become one metalnessRoughnessMap, and a texture's repeat, offset and rotation become the material's uvTransform. Roughness has three.js r187's floor of 0.045. Highlights on small curved shapes widen by Filament's specular anti-aliasing, where three.js adds its own term, so they are a little brighter and narrower there. A normal map that tilts a reflection below the surface fades the environment's reflection, which three.js does not.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial (clearcoat, transmission, sheen, iridescence, anisotropy, specular)
entries.target: materials.standard, with ior, specularIntensity, specularColor and their maps, transmission, clearcoat, sheen, iridescence and anisotropy
entries.notes: materials.standard takes ior, specularIntensity, specularColor, specularIntensityMap and specularColorMap with three.js's names and formulas, transmission, thickness, attenuationColor and attenuationDistance (see the transmission entry), the clear coat and the sheen (see their entries), and iridescence and anisotropy (see their entries).

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial ior / reflectivity / specularIntensity / specularColor / specularIntensityMap / specularColorMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ ior, specularIntensity, specularColor, specularIntensityMap, specularColorMap })
entries.notes: Same names, ranges and formulas, so the values carry over, and glTF's KHR_materials_ior and KHR_materials_specular load into them. specularColor takes linear components above 1, as three.js's Color does. reflectivity has no option: set ior = (1 + 0.4 * reflectivity) / (1 - 0.4 * reflectivity), as three.js converts it.

entries.target: materials.standard({ transmission, thickness, ior, roughness, attenuationColor, attenuationDistance })
entries.notes: Same names, ranges and formulas: the surface samples a mipmapped copy of the opaque objects' colors where its bent ray leaves the volume, as three.js does, and glTF's KHR_materials_transmission and KHR_materials_volume load into them. Give transmission when you create the material, even as 0, to change it later. transmissionMap and thicknessMap take the specular maps' slots, whose red and green scale the transmission and the thickness, so a material with them takes no specular maps and a development build refuses both. dispersion has no option. The copy holds opaque objects only: three.js also draws the back faces of double-sided glass into it. Where the bent ray lands on an opaque object in front of the surface, null3D shows what lies straight behind the surface, and three.js shows that object's color. A custom material sets s.transmission in its surface function.

entries.three: MeshSSSNodeMaterial / SubsurfaceScatteringShader (thicknessColor, thicknessDistortion, thicknessAmbient, thicknessAttenuation, thicknessPower, thicknessScale, thicknessMap)
entries.target: materials.standard({ diffuseTransmission, diffuseTransmissionColor, diffuseTransmissionMap, doubleSided: true }), with subsurfaceRadius and subsurfaceColor for skin
entries.notes: Light from behind a thin surface shows on its front through glTF's diffuse transmission, which glTF's KHR_materials_diffuse_transmission also loads into. Map thicknessColor to diffuseTransmissionColor and thicknessScale to diffuseTransmission, kept from 0 to 1, and a thicknessMap to diffuseTransmissionMap with its value in alpha. three.js's term glows most when the camera looks toward the light, with thicknessDistortion and thicknessPower shaping the glow; null3D's light from behind spreads evenly, as glTF describes, so those two have no option and the glow looks softer head on. thicknessAmbient maps to the ambient and environment light, which shine through by themselves. The front keeps 1 - diffuseTransmission of its diffuse light, where three.js adds the glow on top. A custom material sets s.diffuseTransmission in its surface function. For skin, wax and marble, whose light spreads under the surface, which three.js's term does not draw, add subsurfaceRadius and subsurfaceColor: the subsurface blur spreads the diffuse light on the High and Ultra presets.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial clearcoat / clearcoatRoughness / clearcoatNormalScale / clearcoatMap / clearcoatRoughnessMap / clearcoatNormalMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ clearcoat, clearcoatRoughness, clearcoatNormalScale, clearcoatMap, clearcoatRoughnessMap, clearcoatNormalMap })
entries.notes: Same names, ranges and formulas, and glTF's KHR_materials_clearcoat loads into them. Give a clear coat option when you create the material, even as 0, to change it later. clearcoatMap and clearcoatRoughnessMap must be one texture, with the coat in red and its roughness in green, as glTF packs them: pack two textures into one. A material with a clear coat or a sheen takes no lightMap, specularIntensityMap or specularColorMap. A custom material sets s.clearcoat in its surface function. The car paint add-on builds metal flakes and panel seams over this clear coat, and three.js has no flake lobe: its metal flakes are a normal map.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial iridescence / iridescenceIOR / iridescenceThicknessRange / iridescenceMap / iridescenceThicknessMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ iridescence, iridescenceIor, iridescenceThicknessRange, iridescenceMap, iridescenceThicknessMap })
entries.notes: The same thin-film formulas, and glTF's KHR_materials_iridescence loads into them. three.js names the index of refraction iridescenceIOR and takes its thickness as one range; give iridescenceIor and iridescenceThicknessRange, in nanometers. Give an iridescence option when you create the material to change it later. A material with iridescence takes no lightMap, specularIntensityMap or specularColorMap, and no clear coat's or sheen's maps. A custom material sets s.iridescence, s.iridescenceIor and s.iridescenceThickness in its surface function.

entries.target: materials.standard({ anisotropy, anisotropyRotation, anisotropyMap })
entries.notes: The same anisotropic GGX lobe with three.js's formulas, and glTF's KHR_materials_anisotropy loads into it. A material with anisotropy needs a map, whose texture coordinates give the surface's tangent frame: three.js builds that frame from them too. It takes no lightMap, specularIntensityMap or specularColorMap, and no clear coat's or sheen's maps. Rectangles and tubes of light shade it as three.js does, without the stretch.

entries.three: MeshPhysicalMaterial sheen / sheenColor / sheenRoughness / sheenColorMap / sheenRoughnessMap
entries.target: materials.standard({ sheenColor, sheenRoughness, sheenColorMap, sheenRoughnessMap })
entries.notes: The same Charlie sheen with three.js's formulas, and glTF's KHR_materials_sheen loads into it. There is no sheen option: give sheenColor times three.js's sheen, which defaults to 0, so a three.js material without sheen shows none and its port leaves the sheen options out. Give a sheen option when you create the material to change it later. sheenColorMap and sheenRoughnessMap must be one texture, with the roughness in alpha, as glTF packs them. A material with a clear coat or a sheen takes no lightMap, specularIntensityMap or specularColorMap.

entries.three: DecalGeometry (addon), with a material that has polygonOffset
entries.target: scene.createMesh({ mesh: geometry.box(), material: materials.decal({ map, normalMap, roughness }), position, rotation, scale: size })
entries.notes: No geometry is cut: the box projects the material onto every opaque surface inside it, in a pass after the opaque objects, lit by every light and shadow. DecalGeometry's position, orientation and size become the box's position, rotation and scale. The image lies on the box's x and y sides and looks along its z axis, as DecalGeometry lays it. There is no target mesh: the decal marks every opaque surface in its box. polygonOffset, depthWrite: false and transparent: true are not needed. angleFade and edgeFade fade the decal on surfaces that turn away and near the box's ends, where DecalGeometry stretches the image. A batch of boxes with one decal material draws many decals in one draw. Blended surfaces show no decals. Projected texture libraries, such as three-projected-material, become a large decal box.

entries.target: materials.unlit({ color, map, opacity, alphaMode, vertexColors })
entries.notes: Its map's alpha and the vertex alpha join the opacity, as in three.js.

entries.target: materials.standard with metalness 0 and roughness near 1 (Lambert), or roughness tuned to the Phong shininess
entries.notes: Expect small visual differences: the standard material adds a faint highlight and keeps energy as three.js's MeshStandardMaterial does. Compare screenshots of both versions, then accept or tune.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl, uniforms }) with a toon surface function
entries.notes: Surface functions cannot read the scene's lights in this version. Pass the light direction as a uniform, step the light into bands, and return the result as emissive.

entries.target: debug.view('normals' | 'depth') for debugging; matcap is a surface-function recipe (0.2)
entries.notes: debug.view shades the whole scene, in development builds only. Its normals are in world space, where MeshNormalMaterial's are in view space. Its depth is white at the near plane, on a logarithmic scale for a perspective camera.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl, uniforms, textures }) with a WGSL surface function, or a full WGSL shader
entries.notes: Rewrite in WGSL, in one literal tagged /* wgsl */. Prefer a surface function, so lighting, shadows, fog and instancing keep working. The built-ins that ShaderMaterial adds have WGSL names of their own (see the ShaderMaterial built-ins entry). Declare the uniforms once, as struct Uniforms. Updates such as material.uniforms.uSpeed.value = 2 become material.set({ speed: 2 }), and from 0.2 the type check rejects a name that struct Uniforms lacks. A sampler2D uniform (0.2) becomes var name: texture_2d<f32>; in the WGSL and an entry of the textures option, sampled with textureSample(name, nameSampler, uv). Textures are fixed when the material is created. Full shaders take no textures.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl }) with a surface function or a vertex-offset function
entries.notes: The engine has no shader chunks to patch. Keep the standard options on the new material: defaultSurface applies them. A custom material takes no standard maps (map, normalMap and the rest): declare textures in the WGSL and pass them with the textures option (0.2).

entries.three: A ShaderMaterial that samples the scene's depth texture
entries.target: materials.shader({ sceneInputs: ['sceneDepth'], wgsl }) with sceneDepth(uv) or sceneDistance(uv)
entries.notes: Declare sceneInputs: ['sceneDepth'] and read the opaque scene's depth in the surface function, with uv = input.fragCoord.xy / frame.resolution. The engine binds a copy of the opaque depth. sceneDepth gives 1 at the near plane and 0 at the far plane, and sceneDistance gives the distance in world units. A surface in the opaque pass, or in a scene or reflection pass, reads 0, the far plane.

entries.three: ShaderMaterial built-ins: uv1, gl_FragCoord, gl_InstanceID / instanceIndex, modelMatrix, normalMatrix, viewMatrix, projectionMatrix, cameraNear, cameraFar
entries.target: input.uv1, input.fragCoord, input.instance, object.worldMatrix, object.normalMatrix, camera.view, camera.projection, camera.near, camera.far
entries.notes: The engine works relative to the camera, so its matrices do too. object.worldMatrix has its translation relative to the camera, and camera.view holds the camera's rotation only: camera.projection * camera.view * object.worldMatrix places a vertex, as projectionMatrix * modelViewMatrix does. object.position gives the origin in the world. object.normalMatrix turns normals into world space, where three.js's normalMatrix turns them into view space: multiply by camera.view for view space. camera.projection has reversed depth, 1 at the near plane. input.fragCoord counts from the top left, so gl_FragCoord.y becomes frame.resolution.y - input.fragCoord.y. input.instance is the row in an instance batch, 0 for an object of the scene. object.id and mesh.shaderId tell objects apart, which three.js leaves to uniforms. Only WGSL that reads uv1, instance, an id or the object's matrices pays for them.

entries.target: materials.shader({ wgsl }) with a WGSL surface function
entries.notes: Most TSL nodes map to one WGSL expression; see the shader porting reference.

entries.three: transparent / opacity / alphaTest / depthWrite / depthTest / blending / vertexColors / flatShading
entries.target: alphaMode: 'blend' | 'mask' (with alphaCutoff), depthWrite, depthTest, blending: 'normal' | 'additive' | 'multiply' | 'weighted' (0.2), vertexColors, flatShading
entries.notes: transparent: true becomes alphaMode: 'blend'; alphaTest becomes alphaMode: 'mask' with alphaCutoff; its cut edges are smoothed by default, and alphaToCoverage: false keeps three.js's hard edges. depthTest: false writes no depth either, as in three.js's WebGL renderer. blending takes effect with alphaMode: 'blend' only, where three.js blends an opaque material with additive or multiply blending too. The engine blends in linear color before the tone mapping, as WebGPURenderer does; WebGLRenderer blends after its tone mapping and sRGB encoding, so see-through surfaces look a little lighter in null3D and additive glows a little weaker.

entries.target: alphaMode: 'blend' with blending: 'weighted' on each material that the pass blended
entries.notes: The same weighted blended order-independent transparency (McGuire and Bavoil 2013), with three.js's default weight, the paper's equation 9. three.js's pass takes every transparent material of normal blending without transmission; null3D takes the materials that ask for it. Like three.js's pass, the weighted surfaces blend over the other see-through surfaces, test the scene's depth and write none. The coverage sums -log2(1 - alpha) instead of multiplying 1 - alpha, so both targets blend alike, which compatibility mode needs; the result is the same. The layer draws at one sample on every path, where three.js's matches the scene's samples on WebGPU. weightNode has no counterpart. Custom materials do not take it.

entries.target: doubleSided: true
entries.notes: Fixed when the material is created. A back face lights as if it faced the camera, as in three.js. A double-sided material with alphaMode: 'blend' draws its back faces first, then its front faces, as three.js does (since 0.2). BackSide has no equivalent: flip the geometry.

entries.target: forceSinglePass: true
entries.notes: With alphaMode: 'blend' and doubleSided: true, both faces draw in one draw, in the mesh's triangle order. Fixed when the material is created.

entries.target: alphaMode: 'mask', alphaCutoff (alphaToCoverage is on by default)
entries.notes: The cut edges fade over one pixel above the cutoff and MSAA covers that share of each pixel, as in three.js. null3D turns it on for every mask; alphaToCoverage: false turns it off. Without MSAA it is a plain mask. Without alphaTest, three.js turns raw alpha into coverage: use alphaMode: 'hash' for that look. Fixed when the material is created.

entries.target: alphaMode: 'hash'
entries.notes: Three.js's cells and threshold on each point's place on the mesh, so the alpha sets the share of the surface that draws. The noise pattern differs: null3D hashes each cell with integer math, so every GPU draws the same pattern, where three.js's sine hash changes from GPU to GPU. alphaCutoff has no effect in this mode. A hashed surface casts a hashed shadow, where three.js casts the whole shape.

entries.target: materials.standard({ wireframe: true }), and the same option on unlit and custom materials
entries.notes: Each triangle's edges draw as lines one pixel wide with the material's own shading, from an edge list that the engine keeps for each mesh, as three.js does. Its shadows draw lines too. Flat shading and bump maps have no effect, as in three.js. wireframeLinewidth has no effect, as in three.js on most platforms. Fixed when the material is created.

entries.target: scene.setEnvironment(env); materials.standard({ envIntensity })
entries.notes: One environment lights the scene; a material takes no environment of its own. envMapIntensity becomes `envIntensity`, which multiplies the scene's intensity. three.js uses scene.environmentIntensity in place of envMapIntensity under scene.environment.

entries.target: Nothing to do
entries.notes: Options that change the shader or the pipeline, such as texture maps, vertexColors, doubleSided and flatShading, are fixed when a material is created. Create each variant during loading: a new one compiles a pipeline, which can make a frame late.

entries.target: materials.shadowCatcher({ color, opacity })
entries.notes: The plane shows the main directional light's shadow in the material's color where the shadow falls, and nothing where the light reaches it. The default color is black, as three.js's. Create the mesh with receiveShadows: true, or call setReceiveShadows(true), as the material needs it. Point and spot light shadows do not show on it. The scene's fog leaves it alone. Put the plane just above the surface whose shadows it catches.

entries.target: fog: false in the material options
materials.standard({ bumpMap, bumpScale })
entries.notes: The same formula as three.js: the red channel's change from one pixel to the next bends the normal, so the look is the same, and it depends on the surface's size on screen as three.js's does. A normal map wins over it, as in three.js. bumpScale changes with set. A normal map converted offline (`bunx @null3d/cli assets normal-from-bump bump.png normal.ktx2 --scale <bumpScale>`) costs less at run time.

entries.target: materials.standard({ displacementMap, displacementScale, displacementBias })
entries.notes: Vertices move as in three.js: along the normal by the red channel times the scale, plus the bias, after skinning and morph targets. Shadows and the depth prepass follow, and culling grows each object's bounds by the farthest move, so no setBounds call is needed. One visible difference: without a normalMap or bumpMap, null3D bends the normals by the map's slope, so the light follows the moved surface. three.js keeps the flat mesh's normals, so there a displaced surface without a normal map shades as if it were flat. With a normal map, both engines light it the same. parallax: true adds parallax occlusion mapping from the same map, which three.js does not have.

entries.target: Alpha packed into the base color map's alpha channel offline, or a surface function that sets s.alpha from the texture (0.2)
entries.notes: three.js reads the alpha map from its green channel. Copy that channel into the base color map's alpha, and set alphaMode to 'mask' or 'blend'.

entries.target: A surface function with alphaMode 'mask' that sets alpha to 0 beyond the plane, using input.worldPosition
entries.notes: Pass the plane as a vec4f uniform. Shadows still use the whole mesh, because the shadow pass ignores surface functions.

entries.target: depthBias: { constant, slopeScale } in the material options
entries.notes: Signs differ because WebGPU uses reversed depth: the engine converts, so keep the three.js intent (push away from the camera).

entries.target: toneMapped: false in the material's options, fixed when the material is created
entries.notes: The material keeps its color as the display shows it on both paths. The 8-bit path decides that in the material's own shader. The HDR path's final pass reads a mask of these surfaces and skips the curve where one draws. A blended surface keeps the curve on the HDR path, so draw it on the 8-bit path with hdr: false if it needs the exact color.

entries.target: await assets.loadTexture(url, { colorSpace, flipY, wrap, filter, mipmaps, anisotropy, uvSet, premultipliedAlpha })
entries.notes: It returns a promise of the texture, which draws once its texels upload. flipY is true by default, as in three.js, and colorSpace is 'srgb'.

entries.target: colorSpace: 'srgb' for color maps, 'linear' for data maps
entries.notes: Same rule as three.js: base color and emissive maps are sRGB; normal, roughness, metalness and AO maps are linear. The default is 'srgb' for images and 'linear' for data. glTF models (0.2) set them automatically.

entries.target: flipY in the loadTexture options
entries.notes: The default is true, as in three.js. A KTX2 file takes no flipY: true, so encode it flipped. glTF textures (0.2) never flip.

entries.three: wrapS / wrapT / repeat / offset / rotation / center
entries.target: wrap: 'repeat' | 'clamp' | 'mirror' in the texture options; repeat, offset and rotation go in the material's uvTransform
entries.notes: uvTransform takes three.js's repeat, offset and rotation with the default center, and every map of the material shares it. three.js keeps one transform per texture.

entries.target: filter: 'linear' | 'nearest', mipmaps, anisotropy (capped by the preset)
textures.fromData({ width, height, depth, format, data })
entries.notes: Formats rgba8unorm and rgba16float (a Uint16Array of half floats or a Float32Array). depth above 1 makes a texture array, but materials read only its first layer, and custom materials take textures of one layer only. Filters are linear by default, where three.js's DataTexture is nearest: pass filter: 'nearest'. A Data3DTexture made as a color grading table for LUTPass becomes assets.lutFromData({ size, data }).

entries.three: CanvasTexture (a 2D canvas redrawn at run time)
entries.target: Draw on an OffscreenCanvas in the sketch, then textures.fromCanvas(canvas, { refreshHz }) and texture.refresh(rect)
entries.notes: The sketch worker has no DOM canvas; OffscreenCanvas with a 2D context works in workers. The canvas's last row goes to v = 0, so it stands upright on a plane, as three.js shows a CanvasTexture. In three.js, setting texture.needsUpdate uploads the whole canvas; here refresh uploads only the rectangle. Ask for the 2D context with willReadFrequently: true, so the browser keeps the pixels where the engine reads them.

entries.target: engine.registerVideo(video, { name }) on the page, then textures.fromVideo(name) in the sketch
entries.notes: A video element lives on the page, where it plays with its own controls and sound, so the page owns it and the sketch shows it. The page sends the image of each frame that the video presents, scaled down to maxSize, and the sketch uploads the newest one within the frame's upload budget. A paused video presents no frame, so it costs nothing, and the sketch's call sends the frame that the video holds then. Keep a frame within the upload budget, 2 MiB on Low: 512 texels of a 16:9 video is 576 KiB. Safari and Firefox cannot make a VideoFrame from a video element, so every browser reads frames through createImageBitmap.

entries.target: assets.loadCubemap([px, nx, py, ny, pz, nz]) for sky boxes with scene.setBackground; assets.loadEnvironment for lighting
entries.notes: The faces come in three.js's order and draw as three.js draws a CubeTexture background, mirrored across x. Each face is square, of one size, at most 2,048 pixels a side. A cube map does not light materials and does not blur: for envMap or a blurred background, load an environment from an HDR or EXR image with assets.loadEnvironment.

entries.target: await assets.loadEnvironment('sunset.hdr'), or `bunx @null3d/cli assets env sunset.hdr sunset.ktx2` and assets.loadEnvironment('sunset.ktx2')
entries.notes: One call loads a Radiance (.hdr) or OpenEXR (.exr) file and prefilters it on the GPU, as HDRLoader or EXRLoader with PMREMGenerator.fromEquirectangular do. No loader object and no generator to dispose. The tool's file skips the filtering at load. UltraHDRLoader's JPEG files with gain maps do not load: convert them to .hdr or .exr. EXR files with DWAA or DWAB compression, tiled or multi-part EXR files do not load either.

entries.target: assets.loadTexture('x.ktx2')
entries.notes: Built in: delete the setup. The engine loads the transcoder with the first KTX2 file and picks the device's format. The file's first row is at v = 0, as with KTX2Loader. UASTC HDR files load too: as BC6H where the device has BC formats, else as rgb9e5ufloat, where three.js uses ASTC HDR or half floats. Both stay linear, so keep tone mapping on. The engine also keeps each transcoded texture in the browser's Cache Storage, so a repeat visit skips the transcoder; KTX2Loader transcodes on every visit.

entries.target: assets.loadTexture('x.ktx2'); texture.format names the compressed format
entries.notes: Compressed textures come from KTX2 files of ETC1S or UASTC data, with the file's mip levels. No call takes compressed blocks from code.

entries.three: texture.channel (which UV set a map uses)
entries.target: uvSet: 0 or 1 in the texture's options
entries.notes: Each map of a material reads the set that its texture names. glTF models (0.2) carry this per texture, so loaded models need nothing.

entries.target: loadTexture(url, { premultipliedAlpha: true }), which multiplies each color by its alpha as the image decodes
entries.notes: Blending needs no material flag: the engine blends premultiplied colors. On a blended material, a base color map loaded with premultipliedAlpha: true looks the same as the image loaded without it, because the shader divides its colors by their alpha before it lights them. Other materials show the multiplied colors, as three.js does.

entries.target: const prefab = await assets.loadGltf(url); scene.instantiate(prefab)
entries.notes: A worker parses the file. Named nodes via prefab.find(name), and a copy's objects via instance.find(name); prefab.bounds frames the model. KTX2 textures, WebP and AVIF textures (EXT_texture_webp, EXT_texture_avif) and meshopt compression need no decoder setup. Clips play through the copy's animator: scene.instantiate(prefab).animator().play(name), with the names in prefab.clips. Joints are not objects. Morph targets draw, and clips animate their weights.

entries.target: assets.loadGltf(url, { rewriteUrl: (address) => address })
entries.notes: Checks or changes each address that a glTF file names, for its buffers and images. Return null to refuse the file with E1416. It covers glTF files only.

entries.target: Built in: assets.loadGltf(url) decodes Draco data
entries.notes: Delete the setup and the decoder files. The engine ships Draco's glTF decoder and downloads it, about 60 KB after Brotli, with the first Draco file. Convert the files to meshopt with `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize`: meshopt files decode faster, with a decoder of about 6 KB.

entries.target: Built in: assets.loadGltf(url) decodes meshopt data
entries.notes: Delete the setup. The loader reads KHR_meshopt_compression and EXT_meshopt_compression, and downloads the decoder with the first compressed file.

entries.three: FBXLoader / OBJLoader / MTLLoader / ColladaLoader / STLLoader / PLYLoader / 3DMLoader / USDZLoader
entries.target: Convert to glTF before release: `bunx @null3d/cli assets convert model.fbx model.glb` for FBX, OBJ with MTL, STL and PLY; Blender for Collada, 3DM and USDZ
entries.notes: The engine loads glTF only. The command keeps FBX skins, blend shapes and clips, turns materials into metal-rough ones, and puts units in meters with Y up. Bump maps become normal maps.

entries.target: assets.onProgress((loaded, total) => ...) and assets.preload([...urls])
assets.loadBinary(url), assets.loadJson(url), assets.loadImageBitmap(url)
Nothing to do
entries.notes: Loads of one URL at the same time share one download, files that assets.preload downloaded wait in memory until a load takes them, and the HTTP cache keeps the rest.

entries.target: scene.createInstances(mesh, count, { material, dynamic, colors }); write batch.positions / rotations / scales / colors
entries.notes: Static batches call markDirty(start, count) after writes; dynamic batches upload every frame without it. colors: true adds the colors array: linear RGBA per row, which multiplies the base color and opacity as setColorAt's color does (drawn from step 0.2). scene.createInstances(prefab, count) instances a glTF model (0.2). castShadow and receiveShadow become the castShadows and receiveShadows options, or batch.setCastShadows / setReceiveShadows (0.2). An InstancedMesh's boundingSphere becomes batch.setBoundingRadius(radius) for that batch (0.2); the spheres stay centered on their rows.

entries.target: Nothing special: the engine batches objects that share a mesh and material
entries.notes: Use createInstances for many copies of one mesh, and separate meshes for varied geometry.

entries.target: createInstances(mesh, count, { material, values: true }) adds batch.values, four floats per row, which a custom material's vertexOffset and surface functions read as object.values
entries.notes: Four floats per row replace named attributes: pack a phase, an age, a tint or a size into them. A shader that read an instanced attribute reads object.values.x to .w instead. A material with a vertexOffset casts shadows that follow it.

entries.three: A BufferGeometry with no attributes, drawn from a vertex count in a ShaderMaterial (gl_VertexID and gl_InstanceID)
entries.target: scene.createVertexDraw({ shader, vertices, instances, bounds, ...material options })
entries.notes: The shader makes every vertex from @builtin(vertex_index) and @builtin(instance_index), and the draw holds no mesh data and no per-instance data, so a frame uploads nothing for it. three.js needs a geometry with a placeholder attribute and an InstancedBufferGeometry for the instance count. A draw blends, sorts as one object, takes no texture, casts no shadow, and a raycast does not hit its shapes.

entries.target: baseMesh.setLevels([{ mesh, distance }]) on the base mesh, then draw the base mesh; or levels from `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize --lod`, which assets.loadGltf reads
entries.notes: Levels belong to the mesh, and every object and instance row picks its own level each frame, on the GPU or on job workers, by the level's error, distance or screen coverage. A distance holds on every screen height, and so does a coverage. It measures to the nearest point of an object's bounds, where three.js measures to its position, so a large object switches later. A hand-set level fades over a dithered band, which replaces hysteresis; a level with a measured error switches at once. A mesh whose bound covers fewer pixels than the threshold draws nothing. Shadows draw a coarser level. A level may name a material of its own, so a far level shades more cheaply, such as without a normal map. `object.setLevelBias(bias)` moves one object's threshold, as Godot's `lod_bias` does: above 1 it draws coarser levels, and below 1 it keeps more detail. `object.setDrawRange(start, end)` draws a mesh only inside a band of distances, and fades it at each edge. getCurrentLevel and autoUpdate have no match. Far copies can also draw as impostor cards or as one merged mesh per far cell, from @null3d/impostors. The cards blend the three nearest stored views and light from the normals the bake stores, so a moving sun relights them with the meshes. A large static mesh can also take a tree of cluster patches from `bunx @null3d/cli assets optimize --clusters`: the engine then draws fine patches near the camera and coarse ones far from it, in one draw, on WebGPU. three.js has no equivalent, and its LOD picks one level for the whole object.

entries.three: AnimationMixer / clipAction / play / crossFadeTo / fadeIn / fadeOut / time / setEffectiveWeight / timeScale / mixer.update(dt)
entries.target: const anim = obj.animator(); anim.play('run', { fade: 0.2, loop: true, speed: 1 }); anim.crossFade('walk', 0.3); anim.play('walk', { time: 0.4, weight: 0.7 }); anim.setWeight('walk', 0.5); anim.setLayerWeight(1, 0.5); anim.setTimeScale(0.5); anim.onEvent('finished', handler)
entries.notes: No update call: the engine advances and blends every animator on its job workers. action.time = t before play() becomes play(name, { time: t }). setEffectiveWeight(w) on actions that play together becomes play(name, { weight: w }), then setWeight(name, w): a play with a weight joins its layer's clips, and a play without one fades them out. setWeight leaves a running fade in place, which multiplies the weight. A fade out starts from the clip's current weight, not from full weight. loop: false holds the last frame, as clampWhenFinished does. A clip with a negative speed starts at its end. Filtered clips for upper and lower body become layers with setLayerMask. Walk and run blends whose weights and time scales the code works out from a speed become playBlend and setBlend, which keep the clips in step. crossFadeTo and crossFadeFrom map to crossFade, which keeps the weighted blend that three.js shows; it never uses an inertial transition, which samples only the new clip. startAt has no counterpart: call play at that time.

entries.target: const pulse = scene.animateProperty(lamp, 'light.intensity', { times: [0, 1, 2], values: [0, 5, 0], loop: true }); const recolor = scene.animateProperty(material, 'color', { times: [0, 1], values: [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1] })
entries.notes: A track names a value of a light, a camera, a material or an object: 'light.intensity', 'light.color', 'camera.fov', a material value that setUniform takes, or 'position', 'rotation', 'scale' and 'visible'. Keys hold a number, or three numbers for a color, a position or a scale, or four for a rotation. Interpolation: 'linear', 'step' or glTF's cubic spline ('cubic'), and a cubic key holds an in-tangent, the value and an out-tangent. animation.setTime(t) places the animation, setSpeed, setPaused, setLoop and stop control it, and a material animation changes every object that uses the material. glTF files play their KHR_animation_pointer tracks through the model's animator, with the clip's time, speed, fades and weights: a light's intensity, color and range, a material's values, a node's visibility, and a node's transform or morph weights. A pointer the engine does not read leaves its value as the file has it, with a warning in development builds. three.js needs a plugin for the extension.

entries.three: SkinnedMesh / Skeleton / Bone built by hand
entries.target: Author the skeleton in a modeling tool and export glTF: const hero = scene.instantiate(await assets.loadGltf(url)); hero.animator().play('walk')
entries.notes: Building skeletons in code is not supported, and joints are not objects. Meshes that hang on bones, such as a sword in a hand, follow their joints when the file puts them under the bone. To turn a joint from code, use the animator's joint calls (see the bone rotation entry).

entries.three: bone.quaternion / bone.rotation set after mixer.update(dt); bone.lookAt(target); skeleton.getBoneByName
entries.target: const head = anim.joint('Head'); anim.setJointRotation(head, q, weight); anim.addJointRotation(head, q, weight); anim.lookAt(target, { joints: ['Spine', 'Neck', 'Head'], limit }, weight)
entries.notes: Setting bone.quaternion after the mixer's update becomes setJointRotation, and multiplying it becomes addJointRotation, which turns the joint in its own frame. Turn a bone.rotation Euler into a quaternion with quat.fromEuler first. Both take a weight from 0 to 1 that blends with the animated rotation. A rotation holds in every frame until clearJoint, where three.js's mixer overwrites the bone in its next update. bone.lookAt becomes lookAt, which turns a chain of up to 4 joints toward a point in the world, each within its limit, and aims again every frame until lookAt(null). The joints below follow, so a held rifle aims with the arms.

entries.target: anim.play(name, { additive: true }) for makeClipAdditive. Split clips for subclip in the modeling tool
entries.notes: An additive play adds the clip's change from its first frame, as makeClipAdditive does with its default reference frame. The engine makes the additive form once, at the first additive play.

entries.target: camera.screenToRay(x, y, ray); scene.raycast(ray.origin, ray.direction, { layers }, hit)
entries.notes: scene.raycast writes the closest hit into a hit object that you create once, and scene.raycastAll writes every hit, nearest first, into an array. A hit has object, instance (instanceId), point, normal, distance and triangle (faceIndex), and uv (intersection.uv) with hasUv, which says whether the hit triangle has texture coordinates. The layer mask defaults to layer 0 alone, as Raycaster's does, and the whole scene is tested. Hidden objects are never hit. A skinned mesh is tested in its bind pose, not its animated pose. camera.screenToRay uses the camera of the frame on screen at the pointer's event. For clicks and hover on objects, obj.on('click', fn) casts the ray itself. Acceleration structures are built in. Rays hit sprites, points and lines as they draw. params.Points.threshold and params.Line.threshold become the pointThreshold and lineThreshold options. Sprites, points and lines sized in pixels use the active camera, or the camera of the event's frame, in place of raycaster.camera. three.js's Line2 and LineSegments2 ignore raycaster.far; maxDistance limits every null3D hit, lines too.

entries.three: DOM pointer, mouse, touch and keyboard listeners
entries.target: input.pointer, input.isDown('KeyW'), input.wasPressed('Mouse0'), input.touches, input.actions.define(); obj.on('click' | 'pointerdown' | 'pointerup' | 'pointermove' | 'pointerenter' | 'pointerleave', fn) (0.2)
entries.notes: The page forwards pointer, touch, keyboard and gamepad input to the sketch, which reads it once per frame and adds no DOM listeners. Keys take KeyboardEvent.code names, and the main mouse button or a tap is Mouse0. A canvas that takes touch gestures needs touch-action: none in its CSS. obj.on replaces a canvas listener that raycasts: the closest object under the pointer gets the event, then its parents.

entries.target: createOrbitControls(ctx, camera, { target, enableDamping, dampingFactor, minDistance, maxDistance, maxPolarAngle }) or createMapControls(ctx, camera) from @null3d/controls; controls.update(dt) in onUpdate
entries.notes: Option names and defaults match OrbitControls and MapControls, and mouseButtons and touches take strings such as 'rotate' and 'dolly-pan'. There is no DOM element, dispose or change event: update(dt) returns true when the camera moved. For keys, call controls.pan or controls.rotateLeft with the input the sketch reads. An orthographic camera zooms by its view height, and minZoom and maxZoom count zoom as three.js does from the height when the controls start. zoomToCursor, keys, listenToKeyEvents, saveState and reset are not built yet. Trackball and Arcball come after 1.0.

entries.target: createFlyControls(ctx, camera, { movementSpeed, rollSpeed, dragToLook, autoForward }) or createFirstPersonControls(ctx, camera, { movementSpeed, lookSpeed, pointerSpeed, minPolarAngle, maxPolarAngle }) from @null3d/controls; controls.update(dt) in onUpdate
entries.notes: Option names and defaults match FlyControls, FirstPersonControls and PointerLockControls. First-person controls take the place of both FirstPersonControls and PointerLockControls: while the canvas holds the pointer lock, the mouse turns the view as PointerLockControls turn it. The page asks for the lock in a click handler with engine.requestPointerLock(), and the sketch reads input.pointer.locked; lock(), unlock(), isLocked and the lock and unlock events have no equivalent. For code that moves the camera itself, set movementSpeed: 0 and call controls.moveForward and controls.moveRight. There is no DOM element, dispose or change event: update(dt) returns true when the camera moved.

entries.target: createTransformControls(ctx, camera, { mode, space, size, showX, showY, showZ, translationSnap, rotationSnap, scaleSnap }) from @null3d/controls, then attach(object) and controls.update(dt) in onUpdate; createDragControls(ctx, camera, objects, { recursive, transformGroup, rotateSpeed, mouseButtons, touches })
entries.notes: Option names and defaults match TransformControls and DragControls. There is no DOM element, getHelper or event: the controls make their handles in the scene, report dragging, axis, hovered and state, and update(dt) returns true when it moved something. A gizmo turns an object by the exact angle that the pointer sweeps around the axis, where three.js scales a linear approximation of it. minX to maxZ and showXY, showYZ and showXZ are not built yet, and showX, showY and showZ hide the plane handles too. A press on a handle reaches the handle alone, so a click handler on the object behind it does not hear it.

entries.three: AxesHelper / GridHelper / BoxHelper / Box3Helper / ArrowHelper / CameraHelper / light helpers / SkeletonHelper / PlaneHelper
entries.target: debug.axes, debug.grid, debug.box, debug.sphere, debug.arrow, debug.frustum, debug.light, debug.skeleton
entries.notes: Call them in onUpdate: each call draws for one frame. Debug drawing exists in development builds only. debug.grid takes GridHelper's size and divisions. debug.box takes a box's lowest and highest corners. debug.light draws directional lights only. debug.skeleton draws an animated object's skin joints, blue at the joint and green at its parent, as SkeletonHelper does. PlaneHelper and PolarGridHelper have no equivalent.

entries.three: new Vector3 / Quaternion / Matrix4 / Euler / Color / Box3 / Sphere / Ray / Plane
entries.target: Plain arrays and the vec3, quat, mat4 and color helpers from @null3d/engine, such as vec3.add(out, a, b) and quat.slerp(out, a, b, t)
entries.notes: Create scratch arrays once with vec3.create(), quat.create() or mat4.create(), outside onUpdate. Most names match three.js. applyQuaternion is vec3.transformQuat, applyMatrix4 is vec3.transformMat4, multiplyScalar is vec3.scale and addScaledVector is vec3.scaleAndAdd. setFromUnitVectors is quat.rotationTo, and setFromEuler is quat.fromEuler, in radians. There are no helpers for Box3, Sphere, Ray or Plane. three.js math classes may stay in setup code during a port, but not in per-frame code.

entries.target: onUpdate(dt) or ctx.time.dt, and ctx.time.now
entries.notes: getDelta() becomes the dt that onUpdate gets, also in ctx.time.dt, and getElapsedTime() becomes ctx.time.now. Sketch time stops while the engine is paused or the page is hidden. A fixed-step simulation, such as world.step(1 / 60), moves to onFixedUpdate.

entries.three: MathUtils (degToRad, clamp, lerp, damp, randFloat, seededRandom)
entries.target: math.degToRad, radToDeg, clamp, lerp, inverseLerp, mapLinear, damp, smoothstep, euclideanModulo, randFloat, randInt and randFloatSpread; math.seed and math.random
entries.notes: Same names and arithmetic. The random helpers draw from math.random, which hold mode seeds. MathUtils.seededRandom(s) becomes math.seed(s) once, then math.random(). smootherstep, pingpong, generateUUID and the power of two helpers have no equivalent.
