entries.target: '#rrggbb' or '#rgb' strings, 0xrrggbb numbers, or [r, g, b] linear arrays from 0 to 1; color.fromHex, color.fromSrgb and color.fromHsl give linear RGB
entries.notes: Hex values are sRGB, as setHex and setStyle read them, and the engine converts them to linear. [r, g, b] arrays are linear, as setRGB reads them, so the color helpers' results go straight into color options and instance colors. color.fromSrgb converts sRGB components, color.fromHsl gives what setHSL gives, and vec3.lerp blends two colors.

entries.three: EffectComposer / RenderPass / OutputPass / PostProcessing (three/webgpu) / pmndrs postprocessing
entries.target: post.set({ ... })
entries.notes: The chain is built in and merged into few passes. Delete the composer, RenderPass and OutputPass; keep only each pass's settings.

entries.target: post.set({ bloom: { intensity, threshold, knee, blend, weights } })
entries.notes: null3D draws bloom through a chain of mip levels whose glow keeps its size as a share of the screen, so the settings map rather than copy. UnrealBloomPass: blend 'add', the same threshold, knee 0.01, intensity about 8.8 x strength, and weights from radius (the port skill's table, or its map-bloom.mjs script for the app's canvas size). The bloom() node: the same at a third of the intensity. pmndrs BloomEffect: blend 'screen', intensity as is, luminanceThreshold becomes threshold and luminanceSmoothing becomes knee, weights from radius and levels. Drop the resolution argument. The match holds at one canvas size, 1080 pixels on the shorter side by default; three.js's glow spans pixels, so on a larger screen null3D's looks wider. A strong bloom also spreads a little wider at the frame's edges than three.js's, whose faint haze fades toward the corners; lower strength or radius to soften it. In WebGPU's compatibility mode with MSAA, bloom moves the engine to HDR color with FXAA.

entries.target: post.set({ ao: { radius, thickness, distanceExponent, distanceFalloff, scale, samples, intensity } })
entries.notes: GTAOPass's search and denoise at half resolution, with its setting names; blendIntensity becomes intensity, and distanceFallOff is spelled distanceFalloff. It darkens only the ambient light, where GTAOPass darkens the whole image. It draws where the quality setting aoScale is above 0: on High and Ultra, or after quality.set({ aoScale: 0.5 }) on phones and tablets. For SSAOPass, SAOPass and N8AO, start from the defaults and tune radius and scale by eye.

entries.three: SSGINode / ssgi() (bounce light from the screen) / VXGINode
entries.target: A light probe grid for bounce light (scene.setLightProbeGrid), with ambient occlusion (post.set({ ao }))
entries.notes: null3D has no bounce light from the screen and no voxel cone tracing. The probe grid gives colored bounce light everywhere, from objects off the screen too, at a fixed cost per pixel. Light from moving objects reaches it only when the sketch bakes it again.

entries.target: createEngine({ antialias: 'fxaa' }); the quality presets take MSAA 4x from Medium, and FXAA on Low
entries.notes: FXAA runs inside the final pass, where three.js adds FXAAPass after OutputPass. SMAA has no equivalent. TAARenderPass and SSAARenderPass need no pass on a still camera, and sampleLevel has no counterpart: a view that holds still blends jittered frames into a sharper picture by itself and then stops drawing (concepts/post-processing). TAA of a moving view is a prototype that does not ship: the temporal resolve passes the engine's own paths, and its quality against the presets was measured and did not pass (D-206). The engine records each object's motion vectors, which the motion debug view reads.

entries.target: MSAA, which the quality presets take from Medium up, with FXAA on Low
entries.notes: null3D has no temporal anti-aliasing and no temporal upscaler. The temporal resolve's prototype passes the engine's own paths, and its quality against the reference was measured: it does not beat the presets, so no version ships it. Drop the node and keep the scene's MSAA, which TAAUNode had to turn off. For speed on phones, the governor lowers the render scale, and the final pass scales the image up.

entries.target: The render scale: quality.set({ minRenderScale, maxRenderScale })
entries.notes: The engine draws the scene below the canvas size when the render scale is under 1, and its final pass scales the image up with GSR 1, an edge-aware spatial upscaler, which fills FSR 1's role. It has no FSR 1 pass. Sharpening is a setting of its own, post.set({ sharpen }), which draws at the whole canvas's render scale.

entries.target: post.set({ sharpen })
entries.notes: Both sharpen display color with FSR 1's RCAS in the final pass, so the port needs no render target and no pass of its own. three.js scales the sharpening by 2^-sharpness, where 0 sharpens the most and 2 does nothing: set sharpen to that factor, so three.js's default of 0.2 is sharpen: 0.87. null3D damps the sharpening where the ring around a pixel is noise, which three.js does only with denoise: true. It draws at the whole canvas's render scale; below one, the upscale sharpens the image itself.

entries.target: post.set({ outline: { color, hiddenColor, width } }) and mesh.setOutlined(true), or createOutlinePass(ctx, { color, hiddenColor, strength, thickness, glow, pulsePeriod }) from @null3d/three-compat
entries.notes: selectedObjects becomes setOutlined(true) on each mesh, or on a model's copy from scene.instantiate. null3D draws a crisp line of one width in CSS pixels, with no blur. visibleEdgeColor and hiddenEdgeColor become color and hiddenColor. OutlinePass draws its edge at half size, so edgeThickness t becomes width of about 2t. OutlinePass draws a dark brown line around hidden parts by default; null3D draws none until hiddenColor is set, so set hiddenColor: [0.1, 0.04, 0.02], its linear default, to keep it. pmndrs OutlineEffect: xRay: false becomes hiddenColor: false, and its edge is one texel of its mask at resolutionScale, so width is about 1 / resolutionScale. For OutlinePass itself, install @null3d/three-compat and call createOutlinePass(ctx, { color, hiddenColor, strength, thickness, glow, pulsePeriod }): its settings are edgeStrength, edgeThickness, edgeGlow and pulsePeriod, with edgeStrength, edgeThickness and edgeGlow kept as they are, and visibleEdgeColor and hiddenEdgeColor as color and hiddenColor. It draws the soft edge, the glow and the pulse, and it turns the crisp line off. The pattern texture has no setting, the mask reads at half size, and downSampleRatio is fixed at 2. The core's crisp line stays the cheaper choice where a soft edge is not needed. One outline style covers every outlined object in either form. For a soft glow built by hand, a full-screen pass reads the mask with input: 'outlineMask', at scale 0.5, and an effect adds its texture to the scene color; width: 0 drops the crisp line (guides/custom-passes, a soft outline glow).

entries.target: post.set({ dof: { focusDistance, focusPoint, aperture, focalLength, maxBlur, blades } }), with camera.setFocalLength(mm)
entries.notes: The same intent with a camera's lens: the blur grows with the distance from the focus, and the near and far fields blur apart, so a sharp object spreads no halo into a blurred background. BokehPass's focus becomes focusDistance. Its aperture scales the blur with the distance from the focus, and null3D's aperture is an f-number, so pick one by eye, such as 2.8, with the camera's focal length (camera.setFocalLength). maxblur is a share of the canvas's width, and maxBlur of its height, so multiply by the aspect ratio. pmndrs DepthOfFieldEffect: worldFocusDistance becomes focusDistance, a target to focus on becomes focusPoint, and bokehScale becomes maxBlur with the aperture, tuned by eye. It draws where the quality setting dofSamples is above 0: Medium and up, or quality.set({ dofSamples: 16 }) on Low.

entries.three: None built in; pmndrs ToneMappingEffect with ToneMappingMode.REINHARD2_ADAPTIVE (adaptationRate, middleGrey), AdaptiveLuminancePass, AdaptiveToneMappingPass
entries.target: post.set({ autoExposure: { metering, percentiles, centerWeight, speedUp, speedDown, minEv, maxEv, compensation } })
entries.notes: three.js has no automatic exposure; renderer.toneMappingExposure stays post.set({ exposure }), and the eye adapts from it. pmndrs's adaptive tone mapping becomes autoExposure with metering: 'mean'. Its adaptationRate becomes about speedUp and speedDown, and its middleGrey the compensation, log2(middleGrey / 0.18) stops. Its Reinhard curve becomes a custom tone curve. The meter runs on the GPU in the same frame: a histogram on WebGPU, or 16 x 16 cells on WebGL2 and the Low preset (quality setting exposureMeter). It weights the center, adapts at its own speeds for brighter and darker scenes, and stays within minEv and maxEv, in stops from the camera's exposure. Hold mode settles at once, so image tests stay the same. It needs HDR color, as bloom does.

entries.target: post.addEffect({ wgsl, uniforms, textures, order }), or render.addPass({ kind: 'fullscreen', wgsl, writes, size or scale }) for a pass that writes a render target of its own
entries.notes: Rewrite the fragment shader in WGSL as fn effect(input: EffectInput) -> vec4f. texture2D(tDiffuse, vUv) becomes effectColor(input.uv), and pass.uniforms.x.value = v becomes post.setEffectUniform(effect, 'x', v). The engine joins effects that read only their own pixel into one pass. Effects run on linear HDR color before the tone curve. A ShaderPass after OutputPass sees display color, so retune its numbers. The uv's y axis is flipped: replace vUv.y with 1.0 - input.uv.y where direction matters. Other textures of the shader become var name: texture_2d<f32> with the textures option; sample a render pass's texture at effectPassUv(input.uv). A ShaderPass that writes a render target of its own, which a later pass reads, becomes a full-screen pass, with its input image as input: 'sceneColor', or a texture.

entries.three: FilmPass / GlitchPass / HalftonePass / AfterimagePass / DotScreenPass / RenderPixelatedPass
entries.target: A custom effect for each, with post.addEffect
entries.notes: Port each shader as a ShaderPass is ported. Grain and noise sized for display color look weaker on HDR color, so tune them by eye. GlitchPass's random texture becomes a texture of the effect, from textures.fromData, or noise from null3d::noise. AfterimagePass blends in the frame before, which an effect cannot read, so it has no port.

entries.target: post.set({ lut: await assets.loadLut('grade.cube'), lutIntensity }), or a table from assets.lutFromData({ size, data })
entries.notes: LUTPass's intensity becomes lutIntensity. The table grades display color after the tone mapping, as LUTPass after OutputPass does. A Data3DTexture that code fills for LUTPass becomes await assets.lutFromData({ size, data }): the same order, red fastest, with three or four numbers per texel, whose fourth is skipped. Give floats from 0 to 1, so divide 8-bit values by 255. LUTImageLoader's PNG strips are not read: export the grade as a .cube file.

entries.target: post.set({ vignette: { intensity, size, falloff, roundness } })
entries.notes: null3D's vignette multiplies HDR color before the tone mapping, so bright corners darken instead of turning gray. VignetteShader's offset becomes size and darkness becomes intensity; under ACES the default falloff of 2 and roundness of 0 give a close match, and under AgX intensity stays at 1 or less with a falloff of 3. With darkness below 1, three.js also lifts dark corners toward a gray, and null3D does not. The postprocessing library's VignetteEffect maps the same way with its ESKIL technique; its default technique darkens with another curve, so tune intensity and size by eye.

entries.target: post.set({ ssr: { maxDistance, thickness, intensity } }) with quality.set({ ssrScale })
entries.notes: Reflects what the screen shows in smooth opaque surfaces, in place of the environment's reflection, through the material's Fresnel term, where SSRPass adds its reflections over the finished image. maxDistance and thickness keep their names, and opacity becomes intensity. The material's roughness picks the surfaces and blurs their reflections, up to maxRoughness, so selects and blur have no settings. A groundReflector (ReflectorForSSRPass) becomes a reflection pass, which wins on its plane. The ssr() node's resolutionScale becomes the ssrScale quality setting, which is 0 on the Low preset of phones, and its quality becomes ssrSteps, the most steps of each ray. Where a ray hits nothing on the screen, the environment's reflection shows.

entries.target: const pass = render.addPass({ kind: 'reflection', writes: 'water', plane: { point, normal } }); materials.shader({ wgsl, textures: { mirror: textures.fromPass(pass) } }), whose surface function sets s.reflection from reflection_uv
entries.notes: A reflection pass draws the camera's view mirrored across the plane, with an oblique near plane that clips everything below it, as Reflector's clip plane does. The mesh no longer carries the reflection: a custom material reads the texture by screen position with null3d::reflection::reflection_uv and puts it in the surface's reflection, which the engine lights with the material's Fresnel. Reflector's textureWidth and textureHeight become scale, a share of the render size; its color becomes the material's color with metalness 1 and roughness 0. Water's distortionScale becomes the factor on the normal's tilt in reflection_uv's offset, waterColor the material's color and sunColor the scene's sun. Water's normal map becomes ripples in the surface function. The reflection draws the scene's background, the sun's light and shadows, and the point and spot lights that it sees. For a river or a lake, createWater from @null3d/water does this work and adds the soft shore, the foam, the caustics and the view from under the water; a reflection pass stays the way to mirror a floor. Refractor and Water2's refraction become transmission: give the water's custom material transmission and thickness, and its surface function sets s.transmission and its rippled normal.

entries.target: scene.setBackground({ sky: { sunPosition, turbidity, rayleigh, mieCoefficient, mieDirectionalG, cloudCoverage, ... } })
entries.notes: three.js's Sky as the scene's background, with its uniforms' names, defaults and formulas, clouds and sun disc included. Drop the mesh and its scale: the sky draws behind every object. SkyMesh moves its clouds by the renderer's clock; pass the sketch's time as time instead. The sky lights nothing, as in three.js: for its light, `scene.setEnvironment(await assets.skyEnvironment())` follows the sky in place of `pmremGenerator.fromScene`. `timeOfDay(hours)` gives a sky, a sun, fog and an exposure that match each other. For a physical sky with ozone, twilight and haze on distant objects, move to `{ atmosphere }`, which looks different from three.js's sky.

entries.three: A physical sky and aerial perspective (add-ons such as @takram/three-atmosphere: SkyMaterial, AerialPerspectiveEffect)
entries.target: scene.setBackground({ atmosphere: { sunPosition, sunIntensity, rayleigh, haze, ozone, aerialPerspective, metersPerUnit, moonPosition, moonIntensity, stars, cloudCoverage, ... } })
entries.notes: The engine's own physical sky, from Hillaire's lookup tables, with no files to load. One background call draws the sky and hazes every object by its distance, so drop the sky mesh, the precomputed textures and the aerial perspective effect. Set metersPerUnit to the scene's scale, and aerialPerspective above 1 to make a small scene look larger. The sun's light is in the units of a directional light: aim the scene's light at the sun yourself, or take it from timeOfDay(hours, { model: 'physical' }). The sky lights nothing by itself: scene.setEnvironment(await assets.skyEnvironment()) follows it. The Low preset draws the analytic sky in its place.

entries.target: await scene.createSprites({ count, map, atlas, sizeAttenuation, center })
entries.notes: Camera-facing quads drawn in one batch, with typed arrays of positions, sizes, rotations, colors and atlas frames per sprite. The call is async, because the first one downloads the sprite code. Sprites blend by default, as three.js's do. Without size attenuation, sizes are in CSS pixels, not a fraction of the view's height. Raycasts hit each sprite's quad, as Raycaster does, with the active camera in place of raycaster.camera. sprites.on('click', fn) takes pointer events, and the event's instance is the sprite.

entries.target: await scene.createPoints({ positions, colors, size, sizeAttenuation, map })
entries.notes: Points of one size drawn in one batch as squares that face the camera, at any size on every backend. The call is async, because the first one downloads the sprite code. Points are opaque by default, as three.js's are; transparent becomes alphaMode 'blend', and alphaTest becomes alphaMode 'mask' with alphaCutoff. With size attenuation, size is in world units: three.js's size times tan(fov / 2). Without it, size is in CSS pixels, as in three.js. A point does not vanish when its center leaves the screen, as a WebGL point does. Blended points sort back to front. Raycasts hit each point's square by default. The pointThreshold option gives Raycaster.params.Points.threshold's test instead: a hit within that distance of the point, whatever its size. points.on('click', fn) takes pointer events, and the event's instance is the point.

entries.three: Line / LineSegments / LineLoop / LineBasicMaterial / LineDashedMaterial / Line2 / LineMaterial
entries.target: await scene.createLines({ positions, colors, mode, width, worldUnits, dashed })
entries.notes: Segments between points drawn in one batch as quads with round ends, as Line2 draws them, at any width on every backend. mode 'strip', 'loop' or 'segments' replaces Line, LineLoop and LineSegments, and width replaces linewidth, in CSS pixels or with worldUnits. A one-pixel Line ports as width 1. Point colors are linear RGB, stored at 8 bits per channel. dashed and the dash values replace LineDashedMaterial and computeLineDistances. The call is async, because the first one downloads the line code. lit: true shades lines with the scene's lights. Raycasts hit a segment within half its width, as Line2 does, in pixels through the active camera or in world units. The lineThreshold option gives Raycaster.params.Line.threshold's test instead, as for Line. maxDistance limits line hits too, though three.js's Line2 ignores raycaster.far. lines.on('click', fn) takes pointer events, and the event's instance is the segment.

entries.three: Points or InstancedMesh particles moved on the CPU / three.quarks ParticleSystem / three-nebula
entries.target: await createParticles(ctx, { rate, bursts, lifetime, shape, speed, gravity, drag, wind, turbulence, size, colors, alphaOverLife, blending, map, flipbook }) from @null3d/particles; system.update() in onLateUpdate
entries.notes: three.js has no particle system. A port replaces the loop that moves Points or InstancedMesh rows with an emitter whose particles the GPU moves in closed form: gravity, drag toward the wind, turbulence and a ground that bounces them. Write the effect's look as curves over life in place of per-frame color and size code. AdditiveBlending becomes blending 'additive'; particles never write depth. A sprite atlas becomes map with flipbook. three.quarks's sub-emitters become subEmitters on 'death' or 'ground'. A system does not sort its own particles, cast shadows or take light.

entries.three: A PlaneGeometry displaced on the CPU, with heights from ImprovedNoise or a height map
entries.target: createTerrain(ctx, { size, height, layers, splat, maxLevel, split }) from @null3d/terrain; terrain.update(cameraX, cameraZ) in onUpdate; terrain.heightAt(x, z)
entries.notes: A port replaces one displaced grid with a height field drawn as a camera-centerd quadtree of blocks: the ground near the camera keeps fine detail, the far hills draw coarse blocks, and a skirt around each block hides the seam where two levels meet. Up to four tiled layers blend by a splat map, which the add-on fills by default from the height and the slope, in place of a hand-painted or vertex-colored ground. The terrain carries no collision, so a port that walked on the ground reads heightAt and normalAt to place objects instead of a physics collider. A port that morphed two levels on the GPU keeps its own morph; this add-on draws the levels as they are and closes the seam with the skirt.

entries.three: A tree model per species loaded from a glTF file, or a procedural plant from an add-on such as Sapling or ez-tree
entries.target: generatePlant(species, { seed, variant }) from @null3d/vegetation; bakePlantAtlases(ctx) and plantMaterial(ctx, { atlases, part, cell, color }) for the bark and the leaves; geometry.fromArrays(part.arrays) for each part of a level; mesh.setLevels(lower) for the levels below the first
entries.notes: three.js has no plant system. A port replaces a model file or a private generator with a species record and a seed: the add-on grows the skeleton, the branches, the leaf cards and the lower levels at first use, in a job worker, so the page downloads no plant. A record holds numbers only, so a themed set is a list of records. The asset carries wind bytes in the vertex colors, a pivot record for each branch, the crown's bounds and the source that a far card bakes from; the bark and leaf atlases are painted on the GPU at first use, so a port needs no texture file, and the material that draws them is the add-on's own. A generated plant keeps whole levels, never cluster levels.

entries.target: Sketch: ui.trackLabel(obj, 'hp-12', { offset: [0, 2, 0] }). Page: engine.labels.bind('hp-12', element). A plane of the scene: ui.trackLabel(obj, 'card', { transform: 'world' }), or 'billboard' with a rotation
entries.notes: The sketch places each label with the camera of each frame, and the page moves the element over it in the frame on screen; no messages per frame. The element's center sits where CSS2DRenderer puts a CSS2DObject's, and the offset turns and scales with the object, as a CSS2DObject's position does under its parent. Put the elements in a container that covers the canvas. Hidden labels get visibility: hidden, not display: none. No z-index by distance, and no center. For CSS3DRenderer, a label with transform 'world' takes a CSS3DObject's matrix and 'billboard' takes a CSS3DSprite's, with rotation2D as rotation: the page moves the element into a container inside its parent, which holds the camera's perspective, and turns the element with its world matrix, as CSS3DRenderer draws it. An element is sized in CSS pixels, which are the scene's units. The engine hides a plane whose anchor is behind the camera or outside the near and far planes, which CSS3DRenderer does not do, and it leaves the pointer to your CSS, so give an element pointer-events: auto for the clicks that CSS3DRenderer gives it. It writes a transform only when it changes, and a page holds its planes with maxLabels3d. three.js's css3d_periodictable example ports directly: one object and one ui.trackLabel(object, id, { transform: 'world' }) for each cell, the cell's HTML in the element, and the example's camera; the port skill's architecture guide shows it.

entries.target: const splats = await createSplats(ctx, { url }) from @null3d/splats; assets.loadGltf for a KHR_gaussian_splatting model
entries.notes: Importing @null3d/splats registers the KHR_gaussian_splatting reader, so a glTF model of splats loads with assets.loadGltf. An SPZ file loads through createSplats, which cuts the cloud into detail levels, chooses the splats that draw within a budget that follows the quality preset and the GPU path, and lets the engine sort them by depth. A large cloud loads as a splat stream: createSplats reads an index of chunk files and downloads only the chunks that the view needs, so the cloud draws before its whole file arrives. three.js has no equivalent. Update them once in each frame with splats.update(eye), from the camera's getPosition. The first spherical-harmonic band gives each splat's color; higher bands are ignored. three.js's GaussianSplat and its loaders are add-ons, so each name maps to this one add-on.
